## Introduction

[Adaptive Parameter Optimization](adaptive-sweep.qmd) searches for **one best**
parameter set. Parameter estimation, or *inverse modelling* [@hartig2011],
usually needs more: the **distribution** of parameter values consistent with
what was observed. Quite different combinations can reproduce the same data, and
reporting only one of them hides that.

Approximate Bayesian computation (ABC) estimates that distribution from
simulations alone, without writing down a likelihood:

1. Draw parameter sets from a **prior** (the plausible ranges).
2. Simulate each one and reduce the output to a few **summary statistics**.
3. Accept the sets whose summaries fall within a **tolerance** of the observed
   ones. The accepted sets are a sample from an approximate posterior.

Sequential Monte Carlo ABC (SMC-ABC) [@toni2009; @beaumont2009] does this in
**generations**: each draws new sets near the ones accepted before and tightens
the tolerance, and importance weights correct for where it chose to look.

The result approximates $p(\theta \mid S_\text{obs})$, the posterior given the
summary statistics, not $p(\theta \mid D_\text{obs})$, the posterior given the
full data. The two coincide only if the statistics are sufficient and the
tolerance shrinks to zero [@hartig2011; @cranmer2020]. With a nonzero tolerance
the result is pulled toward the prior and is typically wider than the exact
posterior.

`SbiStrategy` runs SMC-ABC (or rejection ABC) from the
[sbi](https://sbi.readthedocs.io/) package [@boelts2025]. **sbi owns the
algorithm**: the proposals, weights and tolerance schedule. **joshpy owns the
simulations**: each batch sbi proposes is rendered, run, registered, loaded and
summarized, exactly like a sweep. The registry is the only database.

This tutorial is a **known-truth (recovery) test**: we simulate
*pseudo-observed* data at parameter values we choose, then check whether ABC
recovers them. Run this kind of test before pointing the method at field data.

**Prerequisites**:

- Familiarity with [SweepManager Workflow](sweep-manager.qmd) and
  [Adaptive Parameter Optimization](adaptive-sweep.qmd)
- The `sbi` extra. sbi depends on PyTorch; install the CPU-only build first so
  pip doesn't fetch CUDA wheels:

```bash
pip install torch --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cpu
pip install "joshpy[sbi]"
```

::: {.callout-note}
## Runtime

This page runs about 730 simulations of a small model (roughly 40 minutes on a
laptop, one simulation at a time). The rendered results are cached. On a cluster
the same code runs each batch in parallel; see [Scaling Up](#scaling-up).
:::

## Concepts and Notation

::: {.callout-note}
## Notation

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| $\theta$ | Model parameters ($\varphi$ in @hartig2011) |
| $D_\text{obs}$, $D_\text{sim}$ | Observed and simulated data |
| $S_\text{obs}$, $S_\text{sim}$ | Their summary statistics |
| $d(\cdot, \cdot)$ | Distance between summaries |
| $\varepsilon$ | Tolerance |
| $p(\theta)$ | Prior |
| $p(D_\text{obs} \mid \theta)$ | Likelihood, intractable for a stochastic simulator |
| $p(\theta \mid S_\text{obs})$ | The posterior ABC approximates |
:::

@hartig2011 describe inference for stochastic simulation models in three steps,
and this tutorial follows them:

| Principle | What it does | Where |
|-----------|--------------|-------|
| Aggregation | Reduces simulated and observed data to summary statistics $S$ | [Step 1](#step-1-choose-summary-statistics) |
| Likelihood approximation | Approximates $p(S_\text{obs} \mid \theta)$ from simulations. ABC's kernel uses the probability that a simulation lands within $\varepsilon$: $P\big(d(S_\text{sim}, S_\text{obs}) \le \varepsilon \mid \theta\big)$ | [Steps 4](#step-4-what-the-likelihood-approximation-compares) and [5](#step-5-configure-smc-abc) |
| Sampling | Explores $\theta$ to recover the shape of the posterior | [Step 6](#step-6-run): SMC over generations, with importance weights |

In these terms, SMC-ABC combines a nonparametric likelihood approximation with a
sequential Monte Carlo sampler [@hartig2011]. Two other families are worth
knowing:

- **Parametric approximations**, such as synthetic likelihood [@wood2010], fit a
  distribution (usually a multivariate normal) to replicate summaries at each
  $\theta$. Consider them when the summaries are roughly normal at fixed
  $\theta$.
- **Neural likelihood, ratio and posterior estimators** [@cranmer2020] learn a
  surrogate from simulations. Trained on simulations from the prior, they are
  *amortized*: they apply to a new observation without new simulations. ABC is
  not; a new observation means running the inference again. sbi implements both
  families, and `SbiStrategy` currently runs its ABC methods.

## The Model

We use the ForeverTree model from the Josh paper: ten trees per 16 km cell grow
each year by up to `maxNewGrowth`, scaled by a temperature response and a
precipitation response. Drought slows growth, and `minPrecipImpactPct` sets how
much: at 0% a dry year halts growth, at 100% drought has no effect.

The model is **stochastic**: each tree's growth each year is multiplied by a
draw from a normal distribution with mean 100% and standard deviation 5%. Each
run is therefore one draw from an implicit distribution of outputs,
$p(D_\text{sim} \mid \theta)$, that we can sample but can't write down. That is
why the likelihood is intractable and has to be approximated
[@hartig2011, fig. 2].

These are the two parameters we will infer:

| Parameter | Meaning | Prior |
|-----------|---------|-------|
| `maxNewGrowth` | Maximum height gain per year | Uniform, 0.2 to 2.0 m |
| `minPrecipImpactPct` | Growth retained in the driest years | Uniform, 0 to 100% |

## Put `{run_hash}` in the export path

SbiStrategy runs each batch of parameter sets **before** loading any of them, so
every run needs its own output file:

```josh
exportFiles.patch = "file:///tmp/forevertree_abc_{run_hash}_{replicate}.csv"
```

Without `{run_hash}` (or `{label}`), every run in a batch would write the same
CSV and the wrong rows would be loaded, so joshpy refuses such a batch with an
error.
:::

## Step 1: Choose Summary Statistics

A summary function receives one run and returns a dict of numbers, $S_\text{sim}$.
ABC compares these with $S_\text{obs}$, so they must capture what distinguishes
parameter sets. We use two statistics from the final year:

- the **landscape mean** of tree height;
- the **coefficient of variation between cells**: drier cells fall behind wetter
  ones by an amount that depends on drought sensitivity.

```{python}
FINAL_YEAR = """
    SELECT replicate,
           avg(meanHeight) AS mean_height,
           stddev_samp(meanHeight) / avg(meanHeight) AS height_cv
    FROM cell_data_current
    WHERE run_hash = ?
      AND step = (SELECT max(step) FROM cell_data_current WHERE run_hash = ?)
    GROUP BY replicate
    ORDER BY replicate
"""


def final_year_summaries(registry, run_hash):
    """Landscape mean height (m) and between-cell CV in the final year, per replicate."""
    return registry.conn.execute(FINAL_YEAR, [run_hash, run_hash]).df()


def height_summaries(registry, run_hash, job):
    """Summary statistics of one run (its only replicate)."""
    row = final_year_summaries(registry, run_hash).iloc[0]
    return {"mean_height": float(row["mean_height"]), "height_cv": float(row["height_cv"])}
```

The signature is the same as an Optuna objective's, `(registry, run_hash, job)`,
but it returns a dict instead of one number.

**Are these statistics sufficient?** A statistic is *sufficient* if it keeps all
the information in the data that is relevant to the parameters. Then
$p(\theta \mid S_\text{obs}) = p(\theta \mid D_\text{obs})$. Minimal sufficiency
(the smallest such set of statistics) is desirable but not required
[@hartig2011]. We don't know whether these two statistics are sufficient. The
argument for the CV shows that it is *informative* about drought sensitivity,
which is a weaker claim. Using only the final year also discards the temporal
information in the height trajectories. Sufficiency usually has to be tested on
artificial data [@hartig2011], and
[Step 8](#step-8-testing-sufficiency-with-a-known-truth) does that.

Pattern-oriented modelling makes the same point in ecological terms: its
"patterns" are summary statistics, and combining patterns observed at different
scales is a recognized way to approach sufficiency [@grimm2005; @hartig2011].

**Scaling.** sbi's default distance is Euclidean, which adds up the differences
in each statistic, so a statistic with a larger spread would dominate. Following
@hartig2011, who cite @beaumont2002, we divide each statistic by its standard
deviation across simulations from the prior, so that each contributes
comparably. [Step 3](#step-3-simulate-from-the-prior) computes those standard
deviations.

## Step 2: Simulate the Pseudo-Observed Data

We pick a truth and run the model there once. Its summaries become the
pseudo-observed data $S_\text{obs}$.

This run gets its own seed (`seed=1`), so the page is reproducible. The ABC
simulations below leave `seed` unset, so each one draws its own noise, as
independent realizations of a stochastic model should. If one seed were shared
by every simulation, they would all reuse a single noise realization and the
posterior would ignore the model's stochasticity. `SbiStrategy` warns if
`JobConfig.seed` is set.

```{python}
from joshpy.cli import JoshCLI
from joshpy.jar import JarMode
from joshpy.jobs import ConfigSweepParameter, JobConfig, SweepConfig
from joshpy.registry import RunRegistry
from joshpy.sweep import SweepManager

MODEL_DIR = Path("../../examples/sbi_forevertree")
DATA_DIR = Path("../../examples/demo")
TRUTH = {"maxNewGrowth": 1.0, "minPrecipImpactPct": 40.0}

registry = RunRegistry("sbi_demo.duckdb")
cli = JoshCLI(josh_jar=JarMode.DEV)


def model_config(**kwargs):
    return JobConfig(
        template_path=MODEL_DIR / "forevertree.jshc.j2",
        config_name="forevertree",  # the model reads `config forevertree.*`
        source_path=MODEL_DIR / "forevertree.josh",
        file_mappings={
            "temperature": DATA_DIR / "temperature.jshd",
            "precipitation": DATA_DIR / "precipitation.jshd",
        },
        **kwargs,
    )


def run_at(params, experiment, **kwargs):
    """Run the model at fixed parameters and load the results; returns the job."""
    config = model_config(
        sweep=SweepConfig(
            config_parameters=[
                ConfigSweepParameter(name=name, values=[value]) for name, value in params.items()
            ]
        ),
        **kwargs,
    )
    manager = (
        SweepManager.builder(config)
        .with_registry(registry, experiment_name=experiment)
        .with_cli(cli)
        .build()
    )
    try:
        manager.run(quiet=True)
        manager.load_results(quiet=True)
        return manager.job_set.jobs[0]
    finally:
        manager.cleanup()


truth_job = run_at(TRUTH, "forevertree_truth", seed=1)
observed = height_summaries(registry, truth_job.run_hash, truth_job)

print(f"Pseudo-observed summaries at {TRUTH}:")
for name, value in observed.items():
    print(f"  {name}: {value:.4f}")
```

## Step 3: Simulate from the Prior

Every ABC method starts by simulating from the prior. We run sbi's rejection ABC
(`method="mcabc"`) and keep every draw (`quantile=1.0`), which makes it a plain
prior simulation: 200 parameter sets drawn from $p(\theta)$, each simulated
once. These runs serve twice: here to scale the statistics, and later in
[Calibrating the Inference](#calibrating-the-inference) to check interval
coverage without new simulations.

```{python}
from joshpy.strategies import SbiStrategy

PRIOR = {
    "maxNewGrowth": {"uniform": [0.2, 2.0]},
    "minPrecipImpactPct": {"uniform": [0.0, 100.0]},
}


def run_sbi(summaries, observed, method, method_kwargs, experiment):
    """Run sbi with joshpy as the simulator; returns (SbiResult, session_id)."""
    strategy = SbiStrategy(
        prior=PRIOR,
        summaries=summaries,
        observed=observed,
        method=method,
        method_kwargs=method_kwargs,
        seed=0,  # fixes sbi's proposals, not Josh's noise
    )
    manager = (
        SweepManager.builder(model_config(sweep=SweepConfig(strategy=strategy)))
        .with_registry(registry, experiment_name=experiment)
        .with_cli(cli)
        .build()
    )
    try:
        return manager.run(quiet=True, stop_on_failure=False), manager.session_id
    finally:
        manager.cleanup()


def count_runs():
    return registry.conn.execute("SELECT count(*) FROM job_runs").fetchone()[0]
```

The `SweepConfig` lists no parameters: the prior's keys are the template
variables (`{{ maxNewGrowth }}`, `{{ minPrecipImpactPct }}`).
`stop_on_failure=False` lets a search continue past a failed simulation. Its
summaries become NaN, which sbi never accepts, so a crashed run is treated as
missing rather than as a match.

```{python}
#| include: false
# Docs-build only. reticulate (which executes this page) redirects every logging
# handler's `stream` while capturing output, but torch's stderr handler has a
# read-only `stream` that already follows sys.stderr. Make the redirect a no-op.
def _follow_stderr_quietly():
    # One call, so torch is imported and patched within a single captured statement.
    import sys

    import torch._logging._internal as torch_logging

    torch_logging._StderrHandler.stream = property(
        lambda self: sys.stderr, lambda self, value: None
    )


_follow_stderr_quietly()
```

```{python}
prior_sims, _ = run_sbi(
    height_summaries,
    observed,
    "mcabc",
    {"num_simulations": 200, "quantile": 1.0},  # keep every draw
    "forevertree_prior",
)
if prior_sims.failed:
    raise RuntimeError(f"{prior_sims.failed} prior simulation(s) failed")

prior_table = pd.DataFrame(
    {**job.parameters, **height_summaries(registry, job.run_hash, job)}
    for job, _ in prior_sims.job_results
)
SCALE = prior_table[list(observed)].std().to_dict()

pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "pseudo-observed": observed,
        "prior mean": prior_table[list(observed)].mean(),
        "prior SD (the scale)": SCALE,
    }
).round(4)
```

From here on, summaries are in units of their prior standard deviation:

```{python}
def scaled_height_summaries(registry, run_hash, job):
    """height_summaries in units of each statistic's prior standard deviation."""
    raw = height_summaries(registry, run_hash, job)
    return {name: value / SCALE[name] for name, value in raw.items()}


observed_scaled = {name: value / SCALE[name] for name, value in observed.items()}
```

## Step 4: What the Likelihood Approximation Compares

Before searching, look at what the comparison sees at a single $\theta$. We run
the model 50 more times at the truth, as replicates of one job with their own
seed (`seed=2`), and compare each replicate's summaries with $S_\text{obs}$.

```{python}
import numpy as np

replicate_job = run_at(TRUTH, "forevertree_replicates", seed=2, replicates=50)
replicates = final_year_summaries(registry, replicate_job.run_hash)

scale = pd.Series(SCALE)
obs = pd.Series(observed_scaled)
rep_offset = replicates[scale.index] / scale - obs  # S_sim - S_obs, in prior SDs
rep_distance = np.sqrt((rep_offset**2).sum(axis=1))

print(f"{len(replicates)} replicates at the truth, in prior SDs:")
for name in scale.index:
    print(f"  {name}: replicate SD {rep_offset[name].std():.4f}")
print(f"Distance to S_obs: median {rep_distance.median():.4f}, largest {rep_distance.max():.4f}")
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-replicates
#| fig-cap: "Fifty replicate simulations at the true parameters, in units of each statistic's prior standard deviation. Left and centre: the spread of each statistic around the pseudo-observed value (dashed), which is itself one draw from the same distribution. Right: the fraction of replicates within ε of the pseudo-observed summaries, the indicator-kernel estimate of the ABC likelihood at the truth, as a function of ε."
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

SURFACE, INK, INK_2, MUTED, GRID, AXIS = (
    "#fcfcfb", "#0b0b0b", "#52514e", "#898781", "#e1e0d9", "#c3c2b7",
)
SERIES = "#2a78d6"


def style_axes(ax):
    ax.set_facecolor(SURFACE)
    ax.grid(color=GRID, linewidth=0.6)
    ax.set_axisbelow(True)
    for spine in ax.spines.values():
        spine.set_color(AXIS)
        spine.set_linewidth(0.6)
    ax.tick_params(colors=MUTED, labelcolor=INK_2, labelsize=9)


fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(10, 3.3))
fig.patch.set_facecolor(SURFACE)
for ax, name in zip(axes[:2], scale.index):
    style_axes(ax)
    ax.hist(rep_offset[name], bins=12, color=SERIES, edgecolor=SURFACE)
    ax.axvline(0, color=INK, linestyle="--", linewidth=1.2)
    ax.set_title(name, color=INK, fontsize=10, loc="left")
    ax.set_xlabel(r"$S_\mathrm{sim} - S_\mathrm{obs}$ (prior SDs)", color=INK_2)
axes[0].set_ylabel("replicates", color=INK_2)

distances = np.sort(rep_distance.to_numpy())
fraction = np.arange(1, len(distances) + 1) / len(distances)
style_axes(axes[2])
axes[2].step(np.r_[0, distances], np.r_[0, fraction], where="post", color=SERIES, linewidth=2)
axes[2].set_xlim(0, distances[-1] * 1.15)
axes[2].set_ylim(0, 1.05)
axes[2].set_title("Fraction within ε", color=INK, fontsize=10, loc="left")
axes[2].set_xlabel("tolerance ε (prior SDs)", color=INK_2)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The fraction of replicates within $\varepsilon$ of $S_\text{obs}$ estimates the
ABC likelihood at the truth for that tolerance. SMC-ABC estimates it implicitly
at every $\theta$ it proposes, with one simulation each: a proposal is accepted
with probability $P(d \le \varepsilon \mid \theta)$.

The figure also shows the model's stochasticity. The pseudo-observed data are
one draw from these histograms, not their centre. In ForeverTree the draws lie
close together: the 5% growth noise is averaged over 630 trees (ten in each of
63 cells), so the landscape statistics barely move between replicates. Keep that
in mind when reading the tolerances in Step 6. Once $\varepsilon$ is well above
these distances, the likelihood at the truth is close to 1, and the width of the
ABC posterior reflects the tolerance (the approximation error), not the model's
noise.

## Step 5: Configure SMC-ABC

The likelihood approximation is an **indicator kernel**: a simulation counts as
a match if $d(S_\text{sim}, S_\text{obs}) \le \varepsilon$, where $d$ is the
Euclidean distance between scaled summaries (sbi's `"l2"`).

The tolerance $\varepsilon$ is the approximation error
[@hartig2011, Box 2; @cranmer2020]:

- As $\varepsilon \to 0$ the approximation becomes exact (given sufficient
  statistics), but almost no simulation is accepted.
- A larger $\varepsilon$ trades accuracy for efficiency.
- More summary statistics force a larger $\varepsilon$ for the same acceptance
  rate, because distances grow with the number of dimensions (the curse of
  dimensionality).

@wilkinson2013 gives another reading: the tolerance is an explicit error model
added to the simulator, and ABC is exact for that combined model. This matters
for field data with known observation error, where the tolerance (or a smoother
kernel) can be chosen to match it.

The SMC-ABC settings go straight to sbi's `SMCABC` through `method_kwargs`:

| Setting | Value | Meaning |
|---------|-------|---------|
| `num_initial_pop` | 60 | Draws from the prior in the first generation |
| `num_particles` | 30 | Parameter sets kept in each generation |
| `epsilon_decay` | 0.5 | Each generation halves the tolerance |
| `num_simulations` | 300 | Total budget; the search stops when it's spent |

The first generation keeps the 30 closest of 60 prior draws, and its tolerance
is the largest distance it kept. Each later generation halves the tolerance and
samples until 30 proposals pass. The search stops when the budget is spent, so
**the budget sets the final tolerance**. That tolerance is a choice to report
and justify, not a property of the data.

```{python}
SMC_SETTINGS = {
    "num_initial_pop": 60,
    "num_particles": 30,
    "epsilon_decay": 0.5,
    "num_simulations": 300,
}
```

## Step 6: Run

```{python}
import time

started = time.time()
before = count_runs()
result, session_id = run_sbi(
    scaled_height_summaries, observed_scaled, "smcabc", SMC_SETTINGS, "forevertree_abc"
)
new_runs = count_runs() - before
minutes = (time.time() - started) / 60
if result.failed:
    raise RuntimeError(f"{result.failed} simulation(s) failed")

print(
    f"{len(result.job_results)} evaluations in {minutes:.0f} min: {new_runs} new simulations, "
    f"{len(result.job_results) - new_runs} reused"
)
```

The first generation draws its 60 parameter sets from the prior with the same
seed as Step 3, so they are the first 60 of the 200 prior simulations. Those
runs are already in the registry, so they are reused rather than simulated
again.

Each generation's record shows what tightening the tolerance cost:

```{python}
generations = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "generation": p["generation"],
        "target ε": p["epsilon"],
        "max distance": max(p["distances"]),
        "simulations": p["simulations"],
        "accepted": len(p["run_hashes"]) - p["carried_over"],
        "acceptance": (len(p["run_hashes"]) - p["carried_over"]) / p["simulations"],
        "carried over": p["carried_over"],
    }
    for p in result.populations
)
generations.round(3)
```

`accepted` counts the new particles that met the generation's target
tolerance, and `acceptance` is `accepted / simulations`. The first generation
keeps the closest half of its prior draws by construction. After that,
acceptance falls as the tolerance tightens, which is the cost of precision.

If the budget runs out partway through a generation, sbi fills the last
population with particles carried over from the previous one (its default,
`use_last_pop_samples=True`). Those particles met only the previous tolerance,
so `max distance` can exceed the final target; `carried over` counts them. Pass
`use_last_pop_samples=False` in `method_kwargs` to end on the last complete
generation instead.

SMC concentrates simulations where earlier generations found good fits
[@hartig2011]. Compare it with rejection sampling at the same tolerance, using
the prior simulations from Step 3:

```{python}
final = result.populations[-1]
achieved = max(final["distances"])
prior_distance = np.sqrt(((prior_table[scale.index] / scale - obs) ** 2).sum(axis=1))

print(f"Final target ε {final['epsilon']:.3f}; largest accepted distance {achieved:.3f}")
print(
    f"Acceptance at the final target: {generations['acceptance'].iloc[-1]:.1%} for SMC, "
    f"{(prior_distance <= final['epsilon']).mean():.1%} for draws from the prior"
)
print(
    f"Largest accepted distance = {achieved / rep_distance.max():.0f}x the largest "
    "replicate distance at the truth (Step 4)"
)
```

## Step 7: Results

### The approximate posterior contracts as ε shrinks

```{python}
#| label: fig-generations
#| fig-cap: "Accepted parameter sets in each generation. The axes span the prior and the cross marks the truth. Hollow points, if any, were carried over from the previous generation when the budget ran out."
params_by_hash = {job.run_hash: job.parameters for job, _ in result.job_results}


def population_xy(hashes, params_by_hash):
    params = [params_by_hash[h] for h in hashes]
    return (
        [p["maxNewGrowth"] for p in params],
        [p["minPrecipImpactPct"] for p in params],
    )


def draw_population(ax, hashes, params_by_hash, title, carried=frozenset()):
    style_axes(ax)
    new = [h for h in hashes if h not in carried]
    old = [h for h in hashes if h in carried]
    ax.scatter(
        *population_xy(new, params_by_hash),
        s=36, color=SERIES, edgecolor=SURFACE, linewidth=1.2, zorder=2,
    )
    if old:
        ax.scatter(
            *population_xy(old, params_by_hash),
            s=36, facecolor="none", edgecolor=SERIES, linewidth=1.2, zorder=2,
        )
    ax.scatter(
        [TRUTH["maxNewGrowth"]], [TRUTH["minPrecipImpactPct"]],
        marker="x", s=90, color=INK, linewidth=2, zorder=3,
    )
    ax.annotate(
        "truth", (TRUTH["maxNewGrowth"], TRUTH["minPrecipImpactPct"]),
        xytext=(7, 7), textcoords="offset points", color=INK, fontsize=9,
        bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.15", facecolor=SURFACE, edgecolor="none", alpha=0.85),
        zorder=4,
    )
    ax.set_xlim(0.2, 2.0)
    ax.set_ylim(0, 100)
    ax.set_title(title, color=INK, fontsize=10, loc="left")


def carried_into(populations, t):
    """Members of population t that it carried over from population t - 1."""
    return set(populations[t - 1]["run_hashes"]) & set(populations[t]["run_hashes"]) if t else set()


n = len(result.populations)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, n, figsize=(3.3 * n, 3.4), sharex=True, sharey=True)
fig.patch.set_facecolor(SURFACE)
for t, (ax, population) in enumerate(zip(axes, result.populations)):
    draw_population(
        ax,
        population["run_hashes"],
        params_by_hash,
        f"Generation {population['generation']}  ε = {population['epsilon']:.2f}",
        carried=carried_into(result.populations, t),
    )
    ax.set_xlabel("maxNewGrowth (m/yr)", color=INK_2)
axes[0].set_ylabel("minPrecipImpactPct (%)", color=INK_2)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Contraction toward the truth is what a recovery test with a correctly specified
model should show. With field data, contraction shows that the data are
informative, not that the estimate is right.

### Posterior summary

The final population is a weighted sample from the approximate posterior. For
each parameter we report the weighted mean, the central 90% credible interval,
and that interval's width as a share of the prior's 90% width (how much the data
narrowed it). @malchow2024 compare prior and posterior in the same spirit when
fitting an individual-based model.

```{python}
DECIMALS = {"maxNewGrowth": 2, "minPrecipImpactPct": 0}
PRIOR_WIDTH_90 = {name: 0.9 * (spec["uniform"][1] - spec["uniform"][0]) for name, spec in PRIOR.items()}


def weighted_quantile(values, weights, q):
    order = np.argsort(values)
    cumulative = np.cumsum(weights[order])
    return float(values[order][np.searchsorted(cumulative, q * cumulative[-1])])


def posterior_table(result):
    df = result.to_dataframe()
    weights = df["weight"].to_numpy()
    rows = []
    for name, truth in TRUTH.items():
        values = df[name].to_numpy()
        low, high = (weighted_quantile(values, weights, q) for q in (0.05, 0.95))
        k = DECIMALS[name]
        rows.append({
            "parameter": name,
            "truth": truth,
            "weighted mean": round(float(np.average(values, weights=weights)), k),
            "90% credible interval": f"[{low:.{k}f}, {high:.{k}f}]",
            "width vs prior": f"{(high - low) / PRIOR_WIDTH_90[name]:.0%}",
            "truth inside": low <= truth <= high,
        })
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)


weights = result.to_dataframe()["weight"].to_numpy()
print(f"Effective sample size: {1 / np.sum(weights**2):.0f} of {len(weights)} particles")
posterior_table(result)
```

How to read the table:

- **Credible intervals are marginal.** Each describes one parameter on its own;
  the joint result is the scatter in @fig-generations.
- **The effective sample size** of the importance weights is at most the number
  of particles, and with about 30 particles the interval endpoints carry
  noticeable Monte Carlo error. That is why they are shown to few digits.
- **"Truth inside" is necessary, not sufficient.** One truth inside one interval
  isn't a coverage test. [Calibrating the Inference](#calibrating-the-inference)
  checks coverage across many truths.

`result.to_dataframe()` has one row per final particle: the parameters, its
weight, and the `run_hash` of the simulation it came from.

## Step 8: Testing Sufficiency with a Known Truth

Step 1 couldn't establish that the statistics are sufficient. A known truth lets
us test it: drop a statistic and see what the posterior loses.

Mean height alone can't separate the two parameters. Fast growth with strong
drought sensitivity gives about the same mean height as slow growth with little,
so mean height pins down a combination of the parameters, not each one. In
ecology and hydrology this is called *equifinality* [@beven2006]; statisticians
call it *non-identifiability*.

Run the same search with only the mean:

```{python}
def scaled_mean_height(registry, run_hash, job):
    return {"mean_height": scaled_height_summaries(registry, run_hash, job)["mean_height"]}


before = count_runs()
mean_only, _ = run_sbi(
    scaled_mean_height,
    {"mean_height": observed_scaled["mean_height"]},
    "smcabc",
    SMC_SETTINGS,
    "forevertree_abc_mean_only",
)
print(f"{len(mean_only.job_results)} evaluations, {count_runs() - before} new simulations")
posterior_table(mean_only)
```

Again the first generation's 60 prior draws are reused from the registry.

```{python}
#| label: fig-equifinality
#| fig-cap: "Final populations. With mean height alone (right), accepted sets lie along a ridge of equally good fits; adding the between-cell CV (left) constrains both parameters."
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(7.4, 3.6), sharex=True, sharey=True)
fig.patch.set_facecolor(SURFACE)
for ax, res, title in [
    (axes[0], result, "Mean height + between-cell CV"),
    (axes[1], mean_only, "Mean height only"),
]:
    lookup = {job.run_hash: job.parameters for job, _ in res.job_results}
    last = len(res.populations) - 1
    draw_population(
        ax, res.populations[last]["run_hashes"], lookup, title,
        carried=carried_into(res.populations, last),
    )
    ax.set_xlabel("maxNewGrowth (m/yr)", color=INK_2)
axes[0].set_ylabel("minPrecipImpactPct (%)", color=INK_2)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

for label, res in [("both statistics", result), ("mean only", mean_only)]:
    df = res.to_dataframe()
    r = np.corrcoef(df["maxNewGrowth"], df["minPrecipImpactPct"])[0, 1]
    print(f"Correlation between the parameters ({label}): {r:.2f}")
```

Mean height alone is insufficient for the two parameters jointly: the accepted
sets trace a ridge. When there are fewer informative statistics than
parameters, many parameter combinations fit equally well. Adding parameters
without adding statistics has the same effect.

The marginal intervals can hide this. The truth can sit inside both, and each
margin of a ridge looks like an ordinary, if wide, interval. The pairs plot,
not the interval table, is the diagnostic.

## Step 9: Every Run Is in the Registry

Nothing from the search is stored outside the registry. Every simulation,
accepted or not, is a registered run:

```{python}
configs = registry.get_configs_for_session(session_id)
accepted = set(result.run_hashes)
print(f"Session {session_id}: {len(configs)} parameter sets evaluated, "
      f"{len(accepted)} in the final population")
```

Population members carry run attributes, which are queryable like any others:

```{python}
registry.get_attributes(result.run_hashes[0])
```

`sbi_call` is the simulator call that proposed the run, and `sbi_generation`,
`sbi_weight` and `sbi_distance` describe its place in the latest population
that included it. The session metadata records the search as a whole: settings,
sbi and torch versions, and every population with its tolerance and simulation
count.

```{python}
sbi_meta = registry.get_session(session_id).metadata["sbi"]
print("Recorded:", ", ".join(sorted(sbi_meta)))
print("Versions:", sbi_meta["versions"])
```

Because the parameters and outputs of every run are in one place, other checks
can be applied later without re-simulating, as the next two sections show.

## Resuming an Interrupted Run

The simulations are the expensive part, and joshpy records each one as it
finishes. Rerunning a search with the same seed against the same registry
**replays** it. sbi proposes the same parameter sets, joshpy finds them already
completed and loaded, and returns their stored summaries without simulating. An
interrupted run picks up where it stopped.

Here we rerun the first search in full:

```{python}
before = count_runs()
started = time.time()
replayed, _ = run_sbi(
    scaled_height_summaries, observed_scaled, "smcabc", SMC_SETTINGS, "forevertree_abc"
)
seconds = time.time() - started

print(f"Replayed in {seconds:.0f} s with {count_runs() - before} new simulations")
print("Identical final population:", bool((replayed.samples == result.samples).all()))
```

Replay needs the same seed, sbi version and torch version. If an earlier session
with the same settings ran under different versions, joshpy warns that proposals
may differ. Runs that failed, or that you have marked `bad`, are simulated
again. Replay reuses stored results; the simulations themselves aren't seeded.
So a run that never finished is simulated afresh with new noise. That is still
a valid draw, but later proposals may then differ from the interrupted run's.

## Calibrating the Inference

A recovery test at one truth shows that the method can work. It doesn't show
that its intervals mean what they say. To *calibrate* the inference
[@cranmer2020], repeat the recovery test at many truths drawn from the prior and
check that 90% intervals contain the truth about 90% of the time. This is a
parametric bootstrap; simulation-based calibration [@talts2018] is the standard
recipe, and it checks the whole posterior through rank statistics rather than
one interval.

For SMC-ABC this costs a full search per truth, because its proposals depend on
the observed data. Rejection ABC is cheaper: it filters simulations from the
prior, which don't depend on the data, so one stored set can be re-filtered
against many pseudo-observed datasets without new runs [@cranmer2020].

The 200 prior simulations from Step 3 are such a set. Hold each one out in turn
as pseudo-observed data, accept the 20 closest of the other 199 (rejection ABC
keeping the closest 10%, the rule sbi's `MCABC` applies with `quantile=0.1`),
and see where the held-out parameters fall among the accepted values.

If the inference is calibrated, a held-out value is equally likely to land in
any of the 21 gaps below, between and above the 20 accepted values. This rank
uniformity is what simulation-based calibration tests [@talts2018]. The value
then lands strictly between the smallest and the largest accepted value with
probability 19/21, about 90%, so that range serves as the 90% interval. (The
5th to 95th percentiles of only 20 values would cover less than 90% on average,
even for a calibrated method.) This is leave-one-out cross-validation on the
stored simulations [@csillery2012], scored by coverage:

```{python}
theta = prior_table[list(PRIOR)].to_numpy()
stats = (prior_table[scale.index] / scale).to_numpy()
KEEP = 20  # the closest 10% of the other 199 simulations

inside = np.zeros(len(PRIOR))
for i in range(len(theta)):
    distance = np.sqrt(((stats - stats[i]) ** 2).sum(axis=1))
    distance[i] = np.inf  # hold out the pseudo-observed run
    accepted_theta = theta[np.argsort(distance)[:KEEP]]
    rank = (accepted_theta < theta[i]).sum(axis=0)  # accepted values below the truth
    inside += (rank > 0) & (rank < KEEP)  # strictly between smallest and largest

expected = (KEEP - 1) / (KEEP + 1)
se = np.sqrt(expected * (1 - expected) / len(theta))
print(f"Held-out truths inside the accepted range, over {len(theta)} truths "
      f"({expected:.0%} if calibrated; standard error about {se:.0%}):")
for name, rate in zip(PRIOR, inside / len(theta)):
    print(f"  {name}: {rate:.0%}")
```

Coverage within a few standard errors of 90% is consistent with calibrated
intervals. Coverage well above 90% means the intervals are wider than they need
to be (conservative). That is the expected effect of a nonzero tolerance, which
admits parameter sets that fit less well. Coverage well below 90% means the
intervals are overconfident, which is a red flag. This checks rejection ABC with
these statistics and this tolerance; SMC-ABC's intervals would need the same
test with a full search per truth.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Calibration can't detect a misspecified model

Every check on this page assumes the model generated the data. None of them can
detect that it didn't [@cranmer2020]. For field data, add a **posterior
predictive check**: simulate from the posterior and compare the distribution of
$S_\text{sim}$ with $S_\text{obs}$. Include at least one statistic held out of
the fit, such as the height trajectory over time rather than only the final
year.
:::

## Scaling Up

- **Clusters.** `manager.run(batch_remote=True, target="my-k8s", batch_no_wait=True)`
  dispatches each batch sbi proposes as Kubernetes jobs and polls them. If the
  driving process stops, rerunning it reattaches to the jobs still running.
- **Replicates.** One simulation per $\theta$ gives an unbiased estimate of the
  ABC likelihood, which is what the samplers require [@hartig2011]. Averaging
  several replicates into one summary changes the target: it compares a mean of
  simulations with a single observed realization, so the simulated summaries
  vary less than the data and the posterior comes out too narrow. Use
  multi-replicate summaries only when the statistic is defined the same way for
  the observation, or when it describes a property of the model rather than a
  match to data, such as the stability criterion "most replicates persist". To
  use replicates for a data match, synthetic likelihood [@wood2010] is the
  principled route.
- **Failures.** With `stop_on_failure=False`, a run that crashes (for example
  out of memory) is recorded as failed and never accepted.
- **Rejection ABC.** `method="mcabc"` with `num_simulations` and `quantile` (or
  `eps`) filters one set of prior draws. Its simulations can be re-filtered
  later, as in [Calibrating the Inference](#calibrating-the-inference), but
  rejection sampling becomes impractical beyond roughly 10 to 15 parameters,
  even with Latin hypercube or importance sampling [@hartig2011].
- **Regression adjustment** [@beaumont2002] can partly correct the bias from a
  nonzero tolerance, using each accepted particle's distance and summaries;
  `sbi_distance` and every run's outputs are in the registry. Fit it on
  `result.samples`: `SbiStrategy` doesn't run sbi's own `lra` option, which
  returns parameters that were never simulated.
- **Tolerances, summaries and the distance metric** are scientific choices.
  Write them down, with the scaling of each statistic, before the first real
  run, and check whether the choice of metric changes the result
  [@hartig2011].
